newsitem.title: USA: Va. battlefield bonds to end eight-year skirmish.
newsitem.headline: Va. battlefield bonds to end eight-year skirmish.

text.p: A Virginia county steeped in history voted to issue tax-exempt bonds to protect three aging Civil War battlefields in what appears to be the first such campaign by a historic preservation group.

The Culpeper County board of supervisors voted last week to permit a local authority to issue $5.1 million in bonds to buy the Brandy Station battlefield and two other sites threatened with commercial development.

Fleet Securities Inc said it will underwrite the 10-year bonds, which would be paid back by the Association for Preservation of Civil War Sites (APCWS), a group that fought an eight-year battle to preserve the three Civil War sites.
According to the congressionally created Civil War Sites Advisory Commission, Brandy Station, where the war's largest cavalry battle was fought, needs critical attention.
Also, the National Trust for Historic Preservation in 1993 listed the site as the only battlefield among its 11 "most endangered historic places."

The preservation group will use bond proceeds to buy the 616-acre Brandy Station site and the 152- acre Cedar Mountain battlefied. Bond proceeds also will repay mortgages on land the group bought at another site, the Third Winchester Battlefield.

Greg LiCalzi, senior vice president for Fleet, said the historical preservation group will keep 500 acres at Brandy Station in a "forever pristine" state and use the other 116 acres as a buffer zone overlooking the site.
And APCWS will buy another 1,000 acres around the site currently owned by the Elkwood Downs Limited Partnership, It will immediately resell that acreage to developers, LiCalzi said.
He said APCWS will repay the bonds through "dedicated" fundraising, Fleet said.
LiCalzi said other historically rich cities and counties probably have issued bonds to preserve sites. "(But) this is the only deal ever done for a battlefield site," he said.
John Egertson, Culpeper County planning director, said, the site had been zoned by the county for industrial development and the Elkwood Downs partnership had planned an industrial park.
"What resulted was years of arguments between the developer, the county and preservationists," Egertson said, noting that the county favored development since the battlefield is next to an airport.

Nevertheless, the new pact is a "welcome development," he said. The preservation group has actually "put its money where its mouth is and actually bought the property rather than just being obstructionist," Eggerston said.
"We can actually get some tourism out there," he said. Dennis Frye, president of the preservation group, said the financing opens up "exciting opportunities" for financing preservation in the future.
"Fleet has given us an excellent financial tool. It's a model we'll consider in other locations," Frye said.

LiCalzi said, "This kind of financing is possible for nonprofit organizations that have capital campaigns concurrent with financing programs. They can begin repaying the principal as soon as the money comes in."
Fleet said recently that its goal is to become a major market presence in the mid-Atlantic and Northeast.
